endorsements.quote: To reduce uncertainty and improve patient safety in Clinical AI deployment, stakeholders should adopt a lifecycle-based governance approach: hospitals should appoint an accountable AI governance lead, maintain a model registry with clearly defined intended use, ensure user training/credentialing, and implement continuous post-deployment monitoring for bias, drift, and cybersecurity incidents with predefined suspension/escalation thresholds

clinicians should transparently document when and how AI was used, record the rationale for accepting or overriding outputs, and disclose material AI involvement to patients as part of informed consent when it could influence clinical choices

Physicians using decision support tools must disclose their use to patients, since the existence and nature of the clinical evaluation materially influence the patient’s understanding of their care ( 25 ).

Continuous monitoring of system performance across dimensions such as clinical, safety, and technical dimensions, along with notification of relevant stakeholders in the case of performance failures that continue to occur or manifest is also required ( 19 ).
implement continuous post-deployment monitoring for bias, drift, and cybersecurity incidents with predefined suspension/escalation thresholds

vendors and suppliers should contractually commit to validated performance claims, secure-by-design engineering, version control, timely patching and update/change-control procedures, post-market surveillance with shared incident reporting and root-cause analysis, and clear allocation of responsibilities for data quality versus model performance

Accordingly, the most practical risk-reduction strategy is to hard-wire these duties into governance and contracts—clear intended use, change-control and re-validation triggers, audit rights, incident reporting timelines, and explicit allocation of responsibility for data quality versus model behavior

Clinicians remain anchored to the standard of care in decision-support workflows, so defensibility depends on transparent documentation of AI use and a reasoned basis for accepting or overriding outputs, especially where the system’s limitations are known or disclosed ( 54 ).

unlisted_practices: Regulators should set minimum requirements for auditability, incident reporting, human oversight, and post-market monitoring.
Regulators should harmonize cross-border health-data protections across MENA legal regimes to enable safe regional scale-up.
Hospitals should maintain continued governance of data inputs and data integrity after AI deployment.
Hospitals should establish facility-wide procedures for notification, investigation, remediation, and attribution of responsibility for AI-related harms.

screen.reason: This is a comparative legal analysis and policy/recommendation paper examining legal liability and governance frameworks for clinical AI in nine MENA jurisdictions.
